questions.q: What is the Black-Scholes formula for a European call option?
questions.explain: The call formula is C = S*N(d1) - K*e^(-rT)*N(d2). The fourth option is actually the put formula.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the core assumptions behind the base Black-Scholes model?
options: Volatility and the risk-free rate are constant over the option's life
Volatility varies by strike price to match observed market prices
Markets are frictionless with no transaction costs
questions.explain: Black-Scholes assumes a single constant volatility applies to every strike and expiration. Volatility actually varying by strike is the real-world phenomenon (the volatility smile) that contradicts this assumption, not an assumption of the model itself.

questions.q: What does the existence of a volatility smile or skew in real option markets reveal about Black-Scholes?
options: That the formula is mathematically incorrect and should never be used
That its constant-volatility assumption doesn't hold empirically — different strikes imply different volatilities when solved backward from market prices
That options on different strikes trade on different exchanges
That dividends are always paid on every underlying stock
questions.explain: If Black-Scholes's constant-volatility assumption were literally true, every strike and expiration would imply the same volatility. In practice, implied volatility varies by strike, directly showing the assumption breaks down in real markets.

questions.q: For a European call with S=100, K=100, r=5%, sigma=20%, T=1, d1 and d2 are approximately 0.35 and 0.15. What is the approximate Black-Scholes call price (N(0.35)≈0.637, N(0.15)≈0.560)?
Why is early exercise not a feature the base Black-Scholes formula can handle?
options: Because the model explicitly assumes European-style exercise, where exercise is only possible at expiration
Because American options don't have a strike price
Because Black-Scholes only applies to futures, not options
Because early exercise is illegal in all markets
questions.explain: One of the model's core assumptions is European exercise. Pricing American-style early exercise rights requires numerical methods like the binomial tree from Lesson 13.
